entries.name: A-Frame
entries.use_for: Build VR/AR experiences for the web with HTML-like markup on top of three.js.
entries.why: Easiest entry to WebXR; declarative entity-component system with many community components.
entries.summary: Web framework for browser-based 3D, AR and VR scenes built on three.js. You write scenes as HTML-like tags (a-scene, a-box) using an entity-component architecture, and it handles WebXR boilerplate for headsets, desktop and mobile. Community components add things like physics and particles.
entries.best_for: VR/AR prototypes, WebXR demos and educational projects where HTML markup and drop-in components are preferable to writing three.js directly.
entries.not_for: Not for general 3D apps with complex UI or React/Vue-style component trees (use react-three-fiber or TresJS), or games needing a full engine editor. It renders through a DOM-based entity layer on top of three.js.

entries.name: Babylon.js
entries.use_for: Full 3D rendering and game engine for the web, with physics, XR and an inspector.
entries.why: Batteries-included engine backed by Microsoft, strong WebGPU support and tooling (Playground, Inspector).
entries.summary: Babylon.js is a JavaScript/TypeScript 3D engine that renders scenes into an HTML canvas. You create an Engine and Scene, add cameras, lights and meshes, and run a render loop. It ships on npm with full typings and ES6 packages for tree shaking, plus an online playground, a glTF/.babylon sandbox and exporters for 3ds Max, Maya and Blender.
entries.best_for: Building interactive 3D scenes, games or product viewers in the browser with a full-featured engine, typed APIs and tooling such as the playground, sandbox and DCC exporters.
entries.not_for: Production use of the public CDN, which the README warns is only for learning and experiments; self-host packages instead. Heavier than a minimal WebGL wrapper if you only need simple 2D or a few shapes.

entries.name: Depth Anything 3
entries.use_for: Predict depth and camera poses from one or many images and export 3D results.
entries.why: A single plain transformer with a depth-ray output that beats DA2 and VGGT on its reported benchmarks.
entries.summary: A model that predicts spatially consistent geometry from arbitrary views, with or without known poses. The repo has a Python API, CLI, Gradio gallery, and exports to glb, ply, npz and 3DGS videos.
entries.best_for: Monocular or multi-view depth, pose estimation and turning photos into 3D data.
entries.not_for: CPU-only use or real-time mobile; the API example uses CUDA and large checkpoints. Metric depth needs the metric model or focal-length scaling.

entries.name: drei
entries.use_for: Ready-made helpers (controls, loaders, text, environments) for React Three Fiber.
entries.why: Saves writing common R3F building blocks by hand; maintained by the R3F team.
entries.summary: A collection of ready-made helpers and abstractions for @react-three/fiber: cameras, controls (orbit, scroll, drag, transform), geometry shapes, lines, helpers, loaders and more. It uses three-stdlib instead of three/examples/jsm and has a React Native entry point (without Html and Loader).
entries.best_for: React Three Fiber projects that need common building blocks like camera controls, scroll controls, gizmos, bezier lines and primitives without hand-writing them.
entries.not_for: Only useful with react-three-fiber, so not for vanilla three.js, Vue or Svelte. The README itself is mostly pointers to a separate docs site.

entries.name: Fabric.js
entries.use_for: Interactive object model on canvas: select, transform, serialize, SVG import/export
entries.why: Classic choice for in-browser image and design editors
entries.summary: HTML5 canvas library with an interactive object model: shapes, images and text you can scale, move, rotate, skew and group. It includes filters, gradients, patterns and brushes, imports and exports JPG, PNG, JSON and SVG, and runs in the browser and Node.
entries.best_for: In-browser image or design editors, canvas annotation tools, and server-side canvas rendering in Node where users manipulate objects directly.
entries.not_for: Not a 3D or high-performance sprite/game renderer (see PixiJS). Major versions changed entry points (v5 vs v6), so older tutorials may not match current imports.

entries.name: Filament
entries.use_for: Real-time physically based rendering engine for Android, iOS, desktop and WebGL.
entries.why: Google-maintained PBR renderer that is small enough for mobile apps.
entries.summary: Real-time physically based rendering engine for Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows and WASM. Designed to be small and efficient on Android; distributed as Maven artifacts and release archives with host tools such as the matc material compiler.
entries.best_for: Native mobile or desktop apps needing a compact PBR renderer, especially on Android, or a C++ renderer with a WebAssembly build.
entries.not_for: Not a game engine or JavaScript-first library; requires its asset toolchain (matc and related tools matching the runtime version). Use three.js or Babylon.js for typical web 3D.

entries.name: GPU.js
entries.use_for: Run general-purpose compute kernels on the GPU from JavaScript
entries.why: Transpiles plain JS functions to WebGL/WebGL2 shaders with CPU fallback; the standard way to do GPGPU in browser and Node.
entries.summary: GPGPU library for JavaScript that transpiles plain JS functions into GPU shader code and compiles them, falling back to regular JavaScript when no GPU is available. Works in browsers and Node; the README highlights a newer WebGPU backend with an async-by-default API.
entries.best_for: Accelerating data-parallel computation such as matrix math, image processing and simulations in JS without writing shaders by hand.
entries.not_for: Kernels must be simple JS functions limited to what the transpiler supports; not a graphics renderer or ML framework. Speedups depend on hardware and readback costs.

entries.name: img2threejs
entries.use_for: Have an agent rebuild an object from one reference image as a procedural, animation-ready Three.js model.
entries.why: Scripts handle gating and validation so model tokens go only to visual judgment.
entries.summary: A skill that turns one reference image into a TypeScript THREE.Group factory made from primitives and procedural shaders, with pivots, sockets and colliders. A staged pipeline from blockout to optimization is reviewed visually at each pass. Works under Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode.
entries.best_for: Getting a small, code-only 3D model for a web scene that you can animate.
entries.not_for: Photo-real scans or mesh extraction. The README says it is reconstruction by code, not photogrammetry.

entries.name: Konva
entries.use_for: 2D canvas scene graph with shapes, events and drag-and-drop; React and Vue bindings
entries.why: Most popular 2D canvas framework for interactive editors and diagrams
entries.summary: 2D canvas framework with a scene graph in which each shape has its own events, drag behavior, transforms, animation, caching and export. Official framework packages exist for React, Vue, Svelte and Angular; MIT licensed with no license key.
entries.best_for: Interactive design editors, whiteboards, diagrams, annotation and map-style tools needing draggable, selectable, transformable canvas objects.
entries.not_for: Not for 3D or very large sprite counts (PixiJS fits better). It is a low-level canvas toolkit; a full editor needs more work or a paid product like Polotno.

entries.name: luma.gl
entries.use_for: High-performance WebGL2/WebGPU rendering toolkit for GPU-heavy visualization
entries.why: The GPU layer under deck.gl (vis.gl / OpenJS); WebGPU-ready

license_verified.note: MIT per LICENSE (GitHub cannot classify due to attribution notes)

entries.summary: Modular GPU toolkit for the web with a portable device API close to WebGPU, supporting WebGPU and WebGL 2. Provides shader modules (GLSL/WGSL), PBR materials and lighting, scenegraph and animation primitives, glTF 2.0 support and compute where available.
entries.best_for: Building GPU-heavy visualization or custom rendering pipelines, or working with the vis.gl/deck.gl stack, with a portable WebGPU/WebGL layer.
entries.not_for: Low-level toolkit, not a full game engine or high-level scene framework. The retained scene interface is described as experimental and private.

entries.name: MapAnything
entries.use_for: Reconstruct metric 3D scenes from images, with optional camera calibration, poses or depth.
entries.why: One feed-forward model covers many 3D tasks and other models plug in through one interface.
entries.summary: A research framework from Meta and CMU. A single transformer predicts metric 3D geometry from images and optional extra inputs. It covers data processing, training, inference and profiling, and can swap in models like VGGT and DUSt3R.
entries.best_for: Researchers and engineers who need multi-view 3D reconstruction, depth estimation or model comparison in one codebase.
entries.not_for: A research codebase that needs a GPU and Python ML setup. Not a real-time or browser 3D library.

entries.name: model-viewer
entries.use_for: Drop a 3D glTF model with AR and camera controls into any page via a web component
entries.why: Google's easy path to embedding 3D/AR on the web without writing three.js code
entries.summary: Web component that displays interactive 3D glTF/GLB models in a page with camera controls and AR, with no three.js code required. The repo also contains an effects plugin, docs site, render-fidelity tools and the Space Opera editor.
entries.best_for: Product viewers, e-commerce 3D previews and simple AR embeds where you just need to show a model on a page via an HTML tag.
entries.not_for: Not for custom scenes, game logic or multi-object worlds; it is a single-model viewer. Use three.js or Babylon.js for anything beyond display and AR.

entries.name: Modly
entries.use_for: Generate 3D meshes from photos on your own GPU, with model extensions you can add.
entries.why: Runs image-to-3D models locally and lets each model ship as a GitHub-hosted extension.
entries.summary: An Electron desktop app with a Python backend that turns an image into a 3D mesh using local open models. Model and process extensions are GitHub repos with a manifest.json. Official ones cover Hunyuan3D 2 Mini and TripoSG. Runs on Windows, Linux and Apple Silicon.
entries.best_for: Private, offline image-to-3D work, or writing an extension for a new 3D model.
entries.not_for: Needs a capable GPU (AMD works via ROCm). The license is not stated as a standard one. It is an app, not a library.

entries.name: PixiJS
entries.use_for: Fast 2D rendering on WebGL/WebGPU for interactive graphics and games.
entries.why: The leading 2D renderer for the web; great when you need many sprites with high performance.
entries.summary: 2D rendering library for the web with WebGL and WebGPU renderers. Provides an asset loader, mouse and multi-touch input, text rendering, vector and SVG drawing, dynamic textures, masking, filters and blend modes.
entries.best_for: Games and interactive graphics that need many sprites rendered quickly across devices, with a rich 2D feature set.
entries.not_for: A renderer, not a full game framework: no built-in physics or scene editor. Not for 3D (use three.js) or editable object canvases (Fabric/Konva). WebGPU types depend on your TypeScript version.

entries.name: PlayCanvas Engine
entries.use_for: Lightweight web graphics runtime for 3D apps and games, including Gaussian splats.
entries.why: Fast, small engine with WebGPU and WebXR support; powers the PlayCanvas editor.
entries.summary: Open-source game engine built on WebGL2 and WebGPU for 3D apps, games and visualizations in any browser. Includes Gaussian splat rendering, WebXR, ammo.js physics, state-based animation, input, positional audio, glTF/Draco/Basis asset streaming and TypeScript/JavaScript scripts.
entries.best_for: Lightweight 3D games, product configurators and visualizations that need an engine with XR, physics and Gaussian splatting, optionally with the PlayCanvas editor.
entries.not_for: Physics relies on ammo.js; the visual editor is a separate hosted product. Not a good fit for simple 2D, or if you prefer composing small libraries.

entries.name: postprocessing
entries.use_for: Bloom, SSAO, depth of field and other post effects for three.js
entries.why: Standard post-processing library for three.js, faster than the built-in EffectComposer; powers react-postprocessing
entries.summary: Post-processing library for three.js built around passes and effects: an EffectComposer runs RenderPass and EffectPass to apply bloom, depth of field, SSAO and other fullscreen effects. Recommends specific WebGLRenderer settings and a linear colour workflow.
entries.best_for: Adding bloom, SSAO, DOF and similar effects to a three.js scene with better performance than the built-in EffectComposer.
entries.not_for: three.js only (WebGL renderer); not for other engines. Intermediate buffers use 8-bit sRGB, so colours clamp to [0,1] and HDR-heavy workflows lose precision.

entries.name: React Three Fiber
entries.use_for: Build three.js scenes declaratively as React components.
entries.why: The default way to use three.js in React apps; pairs with drei and the wider pmndrs ecosystem.
entries.summary: React renderer for three.js: you build scenes as JSX components such as <mesh />, which map directly to three.js objects. Works with hooks like useFrame, supports TypeScript and React Native, and exposes new three.js features without library updates.
entries.best_for: React apps with 3D content that should use component state, events and the React ecosystem.
entries.not_for: Must match a React major version (v8 with React 18, v9 with React 19). Not for Vue or Svelte (see TresJS/Threlte), and still requires three.js knowledge.

entries.name: regl
entries.use_for: Functional, stateless WebGL wrapper for custom rendering pipelines
entries.why: Lean, battle-tested WebGL abstraction used in data-viz and research
entries.summary: Functional WebGL wrapper that removes shared state by replacing the API with resources (textures, buffers, FBOs) and commands (full draw-call state). Commands are compiled to optimized JS; includes validation in dev mode and a large unit test suite.
entries.best_for: Custom WebGL rendering, data visualization and research code where you want direct control without scene graph or engine opinions.
entries.not_for: Not a game engine: no scene graph, math or materials. You write shaders yourself and it targets WebGL, not WebGPU.

entries.name: SAM 3D Objects
entries.use_for: Reconstruct a textured 3D model with pose and layout from a single image.
entries.why: Meta model that copes with occlusion and clutter in real photos; code, weights and a benchmark are released.
entries.summary: A foundation model that reconstructs 3D shape, texture and layout from one image. It converts masked objects into 3D models and supports single or multi-object scenes. Python inference code and notebooks are included.
entries.best_for: Turning photos into 3D assets, or researching single-image 3D generation.
entries.not_for: Research code with checkpoints to download and GPU needs. Licence is listed as NOASSERTION, so read it before commercial use.

entries.name: SHARP (ml-sharp)
entries.use_for: Turn one photo into a 3D Gaussian scene you can render from nearby viewpoints in real time.
entries.why: Predicts a metric 3D Gaussian scene from one image in under a second on a GPU.
entries.summary: Reference code for the SHARP paper. A single feedforward pass regresses 3D Gaussian parameters from one photograph. The result renders in real time for nearby camera moves and has absolute scale. A `sharp` CLI is installed with pip.
entries.best_for: Fast single-image novel view synthesis, 3D photo effects, or research that builds on 3D Gaussian scenes.
entries.not_for: Research code, and the license is not stated as a standard open license. It handles nearby views only, not full 360-degree reconstruction.

entries.name: three-mesh-bvh
entries.use_for: Fast raycasting, collision and spatial queries on three.js meshes
entries.why: Go-to BVH acceleration for three.js; used by drei, path tracers and many editors
entries.summary: Bounding volume hierarchy implementation that accelerates raycasting and spatial queries against three.js meshes. Supports skinned geometry, point clouds, lines, shape intersection, SDF generation, web worker builds and BatchedMesh.
entries.best_for: three.js scenes with heavy raycasting or collision such as picking on large meshes, character movement, sculpting tools or path tracers.
entries.not_for: three.js only, and unnecessary for small scenes where default raycasting is fast enough. It adds BVH build time and memory per geometry.

entries.name: three.js
entries.use_for: Render 3D scenes in the browser with WebGL or WebGPU.
entries.why: The standard 3D library for the web, with the largest ecosystem of examples, loaders and add-ons.
entries.summary: General-purpose 3D library for the browser with WebGL and WebGPU renderers (SVG and CSS3D renderers available as addons). Provides scenes, cameras, geometries, materials, loaders and a large set of examples.
entries.best_for: Most browser 3D work: visualizations, product views, games and creative coding, especially if you want the biggest ecosystem of examples and add-ons.
entries.not_for: A rendering library, not a game engine: no built-in physics, editor or ECS. Cloning the full repo is about 2 GB; use shallow clone or npm.

entries.name: Threlte
entries.use_for: Build three.js scenes declaratively in Svelte.
entries.why: The Svelte counterpart to React Three Fiber, with physics and helper packages.
entries.summary: Svelte library for building three.js scenes declaratively with a type-safe, reactive API. Split into packages: core bindings, extras, a glTF-to-component CLI, Rapier physics, Theatre.js animation and XR components.
entries.best_for: Svelte or SvelteKit projects that need 3D, physics or timeline animation with Svelte-native events and reactivity.
entries.not_for: Svelte only; use react-three-fiber for React or TresJS for Vue. Still requires understanding three.js concepts.

entries.name: TRELLIS.2
entries.use_for: Generate PBR-textured 3D assets, exported as GLB, from a single image.
entries.why: 4B-parameter model with sharp features and complex topology; training code is released.
entries.summary: A large 3D generative model using a sparse voxel structure called O-Voxel. A Python pipeline turns an image into a 3D asset and writes a preview video and a GLB file. Texture generation from a given shape is also supported.
entries.best_for: Adding image-to-3D to a pipeline, or researching 3D generation, with open weights and training code.
entries.not_for: CPU-only machines. Python and a capable CUDA GPU are expected, and GLB output is opaque until you wire up alpha.

entries.name: TresJS
entries.use_for: Build three.js scenes declaratively with Vue components.
entries.why: The Vue counterpart to React Three Fiber, with a Nuxt module and helper packages.
entries.summary: Custom Vue renderer that lets you build three.js scenes with Vue components in a declarative, fully typed way. Built on Vite, tracks new three.js features without wrapper updates, with an ecosystem of helper packages.
entries.best_for: Vue and Nuxt apps that want 3D scenes as components using the latest three.js.
entries.not_for: Vue only (use react-three-fiber or Threlte elsewhere). Needs three.js knowledge, and ecosystem packages are separate installs.

entries.name: Two.js
entries.use_for: Renderer-agnostic 2D drawing API that targets SVG, Canvas or WebGL
entries.why: Simple 2D drawing with one API across three renderers
entries.summary: Two-dimensional drawing API for modern browsers that is renderer agnostic: the same code renders to SVG, Canvas2D or WebGL. Installable via script tag or npm, supports ES6 imports and custom builds that exclude unused renderers.
entries.best_for: Simple 2D vector drawing, generative art and animations where you want one API across SVG, canvas and WebGL.
entries.not_for: Not an interactive editor framework (Konva/Fabric) or a high-performance sprite engine (PixiJS); no 3D.

entries.name: TypeGPU
entries.use_for: Write type-safe WebGPU code and shaders in TypeScript.
entries.why: Removes much of WebGPU boilerplate with strong type inference; maintained by Software Mansion.
entries.summary: Modular TypeScript toolkit for WebGPU with strong type inference and the ability to write shaders in TypeScript via a 'use gpu' directive. Mirrors WGSL concepts, can be adopted piecemeal in existing apps and ejected to vanilla WebGPU.
entries.best_for: WebGPU projects wanting type-safe buffers, bind groups and TypeScript-authored shaders with less boilerplate, or libraries that need typed GPU data handling.
entries.not_for: Not a ready-made renderer or engine; you still design the graphics pipeline. Requires WebGPU-capable browsers and familiarity with WebGPU/WGSL concepts.

entries.name: wgpu
entries.use_for: Cross-platform, safe Rust graphics API based on WebGPU, running on Vulkan, Metal, DX12 and the web.
entries.why: Foundation of most Rust graphics (Bevy, Firefox WebGPU); one API across native and browser.
entries.summary: Cross-platform, pure-Rust graphics API based on the WebGPU standard. Runs natively on Vulkan, Metal, D3D12 and OpenGL, and on WebGL2/WebGPU in wasm; it powers WebGPU in Firefox, Servo and Deno.
entries.best_for: Rust apps and engines that need one GPU API across desktop and browser, or learning WebGPU in Rust.
entries.not_for: Low-level graphics API, not an engine or UI toolkit. Rust-centric (C and other bindings exist but are secondary); for JS web apps use WebGPU directly or three.js.
